implementation_notes: Swift has the pattern as a keyword: guard condition else { ... } requires the condition to hold for the rest of the scope, the else branch must transfer control out (return, break, continue, throw, or a non-returning call such as fatalError), and any optional bound in the condition stays available afterwards - the swift-book's Early Exit section states all three points. That combination is what keeps the happy path flat and non-optional. Use guard for input and state the caller can fix, and precondition/assert for invalid program state rather than recoverable errors.
pitfalls: The else branch must exit the scope (return/break/continue/throw/fatalError), so a guard cannot express log and continue; that is what if is for.
guard let introduces a new binding that shadows the optional; using the original instead of the binding is caught by the compiler only if it is still optional.
A failed precondition cannot be caught (the book states recovering from an invalid state is impossible), so preconditions are not guards for user input.

variants.name: Trapping preconditions for invalid program state
variants.implementation_notes: The second Swift realisation guards the opposite category: conditions that indicate a programmer error rather than caller-fixable input. precondition(condition, message) is checked in both debug and production builds, assert only in debug builds, preconditionFailure marks branches that must never be taken, and compiling with -Ounchecked drops the preconditions while fatalError always halts - all documented in the book's Assertions and Preconditions section. Choose traps when continuing would leave the program in an invalid state and no caller can act on the failure; keep guard for anything a caller can cause.
pitfalls: A failed precondition or assertion cannot be caught (the book: recovering from an invalid state is impossible), so using one for user input crashes the process instead of returning an error.
Assertions are compiled out of release builds and preconditions are skipped under -Ounchecked, so neither can enforce a security check; guard plus throw is the form that always runs.
fatalError halts unconditionally even under -Ounchecked; reserve it for stubs and genuinely unreachable code.
